title: The Roll of Defeated Kings
summary: The chapter lists the kings Israel defeated. First come the two kings east of the Jordan, Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan, conquered under Moses, whose lands went to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. Then come thirty-one kings west of the Jordan defeated under Joshua, named one by one from Jericho to Tirzah.
story: Chapter 11 ended with the land at rest; chapter 12 stops to take stock before the land is divided. It works like a closing ledger for the first half of the book. By setting Moses' victories beside Joshua's, it presents the conquest as one work of God across two leaders and two sides of the Jordan, fulfilling what the LORD promised at the burning bush and to Abraham long before. With the enemies listed, the book can turn in chapter 13 to the question of inheritance: who receives which part of the land God has given.
historical:
Sihon and Og were defeated at the end of the wilderness years (Numbers 21:21-35; Deuteronomy 2:26-3:11), and their fall became one of Israel's most remembered victories, recalled in Psalms 135 and 136. Their lands covered the plateau and Gilead east of the Jordan, from the Arnon gorge, which flows into the Dead Sea from the east, north to Mount Hermon. The kings of Hormah and Arad in the Negev recall the battle of Numbers 21:1-3.

The western list includes places whose later importance a first reader would have known. Megiddo guarded the main pass through the Carmel ridge into the Jezreel Valley; Pharaoh Thutmose III fought a famous battle there in the fifteenth century BC, and the name is behind Armageddon in Revelation 16:16. Tirzah became the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel for a time (1 Kings 16:23), before Omri built Samaria. Dor was a port on the Mediterranean coast, Aphek a strategic town at the head of the Yarkon River where the Philistines later camped (1 Samuel 4:1). Some place names in the list are uncertain, and the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint, made in the last centuries BC) differs from the Hebrew in several of them.
cultural:
Ancient Near Eastern kings recorded their conquests in lists. Egyptian pharaohs had the names of conquered towns carved on temple walls, often each name inside an oval representing a bound captive. A list like Joshua 12 served similar purposes for Israel: it was a public record of victory and a legal statement of claim to the territory. The word "king" in these lists means the ruler of a city-state, a fortified town with its surrounding villages and fields. Canaan in this period was a patchwork of such small kingdoms, many of them nominally subject to Egypt, which is why so many kings appear within a small land.

For Israel, the list was also a kind of worship. Naming each defeated king, with the single word "one" after each, invited the reader to count the LORD's victories. The same impulse lies behind the psalms that name Sihon and Og as evidence of God's steadfast love.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-6 describe the eastern conquest under Moses, marked by careful geographical boundaries. Verses 7-24 describe the western conquest under Joshua, first with a general description of the regions (verses 7-8), then with a formal list. In the Hebrew the list is laid out as a column, with each king's name followed by the word "one" (echad), and it ends with a total: thirty-one. The order roughly follows the narrative: Jericho and Ai, then the southern kings of chapter 10, then others in the center and north, including Hazor and its allies from chapter 11. Some kings appear here whose defeat the book never narrates, such as those of Bethel and Tirzah, which shows that the stories in chapters 6-11 are selective rather than complete.

outline.t: Og king of Bashan and the eastern tribes
The lands west of the Jordan

doctrines.note: The list shows the promise to Abraham (Genesis 15:18-21) being kept, city by city. God's faithfulness is not an abstraction but a matter of named places and counted victories.
Placing Moses and Joshua side by side shows one purpose of God carried through a change of leadership. The work did not depend on a single man; the LORD who used Moses continued with Joshua.

words.note: Echad, one. Repeated after every name in the list, it turns a record into a count. The effect is cumulative: one, one, one, until the reader reaches thirty-one and sees how much God has done.

Yerushah, possession. The eastern land was given to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh as a possession (verse 6). The word looks ahead to the following chapters, which are about the land as something received and held, not merely seized.

Melek, king. Used thirty-seven times in this short chapter. In Canaan a king was usually the ruler of a single walled city and its villages. The book's point is that these many kings, each a power in his own place, all fell before the one King, the LORD.

christ: The link is thematic. The chapter is a victory roll, a list of powers that once ruled the land and were overthrown so that God's people could receive their inheritance. The New Testament describes Christ's victory in similar terms: God raised him and seated him far above all rule and authority and power and dominion (Ephesians 1:20-21), and at the cross he disarmed the powers and authorities and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15). Where Joshua's list names Canaanite kings, the New Testament names deeper enemies, sin, death, and the powers of evil, and speaks of an inheritance that is imperishable (1 Peter 1:4).

hard.q: If these kings were all defeated, why do later chapters and Judges say that many of these cities remained in Canaanite hands?
hard.a: Several cities in this list, such as Jerusalem, Gezer, Megiddo, Taanach, and Dor, appear later as places Israel did not take or did not hold (Joshua 15:63; 16:10; 17:11-12; Judges 1:21, 27). Many readers resolve this by distinguishing the defeat of a king or his army from the lasting occupation of his city: a king could be killed in battle while his town survived, was reoccupied, or was never settled by Israel. Others read the list as a summary in the conventional, sweeping style of ancient victory records, which the book itself qualifies. Still others think the book combines sources with different emphases. The book seems aware of the tension, since chapter 13 opens by saying that very much land remained to be possessed.

questions: Why might it matter to write down God's past faithfulness by name and number? What would a list of your own look like?
The chapter treats Moses' victories and Joshua's as one work. How does it help to see your part in God's purposes as continuous with those who came before you?
A king defeated is not always a city possessed. Where have you seen a decisive victory followed by a long, slower work of taking hold of what was won?
